title: The bitter cucumber
hookLine: a cucumber is bitter? put it down; briars in the path? step aside (Meditations 8.50)

lines: A LONG SPEECH ABOUT A SANDWICH.
cards: You bite into a sandwich and the lettuce has gone slimy. You could put it down. Or you could hold it up and say to the room: why?
Why does this always happen? Who packs a sandwich like this? What's wrong with this whole store?
Five minutes later, you're still holding the sandwich. Some of us are very gifted at turning small annoyances into long speeches. Marcus, it seems, knew the habit.
So he gave himself a short, dry bit of advice. It starts with a vegetable.

teach.b: Book Eight, section fifty, in George Long's translation: "A cucumber is bitter. Throw it away. There are briers in the road. Turn aside from them." This is enough, Marcus says.

teach.h: DON'T ADD: WHY WAS THIS MADE?
teach.b: Don't add: and why were such things ever made? The first part is action. Bitter?
Put it down. Thorny path? Go around.
The second part is what not to add: the speech. The why me. The why is the world like this.
Marcus even has a joke about it. Ask why there are bitter cucumbers, he says, and someone who understands nature would laugh at you.
It's like walking into a carpenter's shop and complaining about the wood shavings on the floor, or into a shoemaker's and complaining about the leather scraps. Of course there are scraps.

That's what a workshop looks like when things are being made. For the Stoics, the world is nature's workshop, and bitter cucumbers and briars are some of the shavings. Yesterday was about the judgment you add to a thing.

Some things don't even need a new judgment, just a small movement: put it down, step aside, carry on. You don't have to understand why the cucumber is bitter, fix the briars, or make it mean something about your life.
There's a lightness to it, almost funny. A lot of annoyances are cucumbers. Your line: step aside.

how: Readers of Marcus often use this line for small daily irritations: deal with the thing simply, and skip the added complaint about why the world contains it.

o: a cool food that calms a hot temper
a gift from nature you should always accept
a small bitter thing you just put down and leave

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: what a workshop floor looks like

s: Marcus says you should work out why cucumbers are bitter
he says don't add 'why were such things made'. put it down and move on.
Marcus compares the world to a workshop full of scraps
complaining about bitter cucumbers is like complaining about shavings in a carpenter's shop.
Marcus says a workshop floor is full of scraps
shavings and cuttings are what a carpenter's or shoemaker's shop looks like when things are being made.

games.q: you're walking and the path ahead is full of briars. what does Marcus do?
o: ask why briars were ever made.
turn aside from them and keep walking.
games.why: turn aside from them. this is enough, he writes; don't add a speech about why they exist.

practice: Let a small, familiar annoyance come to mind: the noisy neighbor, the slow app, the sock that's always inside out. Notice the speech that usually comes with it.
Then picture yourself simply putting it down, or stepping around it, with no speech at all, and feel how light that is.

wordCard.voice: Cucumber. Marcus says if a cucumber is bitter, throw it away; if there are briars in the road, turn aside, and don't ask why. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a cucumber. the first word of Marcus's entry on bitter cucumbers.

carryVoice: Your line: step aside. A bitter cucumber doesn't need a speech. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: A cucumber is bitter. Throw it away. There are briers in the road. Turn aside from them.
